pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; identify arithmetic patterns (in the addition/multiplication table) and EXPLAIN them using properties of operations — not just spot them.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4–Y5 'recognise and use … patterns'; explaining patterns using properties supports reasoning across number.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 3.OA.9 — 'identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations. For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.'
• Operational details — the load-bearing verb is EXPLAIN. Children notice patterns (5s end in 0/5; the 9s digits sum to 9; even×anything is even; the multiplication table is symmetric across the diagonal) and then justify them using structure/properties: symmetry = commutativity; every-other-even in a row = the distributive/doubling structure; 5s pattern = 5=half of 10. This moves maths from 'noticing' to 'reasoning why', the heart of early mathematical argument. Use the multiplication square and colour/highlighting to surface patterns, then press for a structural explanation, not just a restatement.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): spot a pattern (all 5s end in 0 or 5; the 2s are all even). Tier B (age 8–9): explain a pattern using structure ('4×n is always even because it's double 2n'). Tier C (age 9): explain the table's diagonal symmetry using commutativity and predict/extend a pattern.
bestPractices: Demand explanation, not just noticing — always ask 'why does that happen?' and accept a structural/property-based reason, not a restatement of the pattern.
Use the multiplication square with colour-coding to make patterns visible (shade multiples, the diagonal of squares, the symmetric pairs).
Link each pattern to its property: table symmetry → commutativity; 4×n even → doubling/distributive; 5s → half of 10s.
Encourage prediction — 'if the pattern holds, what comes next?' — then verify, building conjecture-and-check habits.
Connect number patterns to the addition table too, and to later shape/number sequence work.
keyRepresentations: Multiplication square with colour-coded multiples and the symmetry diagonal
Array/doubling diagrams to justify 'even' and step patterns
commonMisconceptions: Describing a pattern but 'explaining' it by restating it rather than giving a structural reason.
Over-generalising a pattern beyond where it holds without checking.
Missing that the multiplication table is symmetric (not linking it to commutativity).
Thinking a pattern is coincidence rather than a consequence of properties.
Confusing multiples patterns with place-value digit patterns without understanding the cause.

learn.summary: For 8–9 year olds: identify arithmetic patterns in the addition/multiplication tables AND explain them using the structure of operations — moving from 'noticing' to 'reasoning why'. The load-bearing verb is EXPLAIN: a child should justify a pattern using a structural reason (the table is symmetric because of commutativity, a×b = b×a; 4×n is even because it is double 2n; multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5 because 5 is half of 10 / each +5 step moves the ones digit between 5 and 0), not merely restate the observation. A colour-coded multiplication square that the learner can shade, fold across the diagonal and decompose makes the structure visible and interrogable; a Socratic 'why?' partner pushes explanation past description.

activities.title: Shade, fold and decompose the multiplication square
feedback: If the child only restates ('because it's the 5 times table'), press on the +5 step: show the ones digit going 5, 0, 5, 0 as you add five each time — that alternation is the reason.

If the child thinks a pattern might break for large multiples, reason from the repeating +5 step, which never changes, so the ones-digit cycle continues; test a large case such as 5×70 (=350) to reassure.

When the child folds the whole table onto itself and sees every cell meet its mirror, name the reason: the symmetry happens because of commutativity (a×b = b×a) — swapping the order of the two factors never changes the product, so each cell equals its mirror cell.
activities.rationale: Manipulating structure on the same surface where the pattern appears lets conjecture and justification happen together, supporting the standard's demand to explain patterns using properties of operations. A live interactive grid is one effective medium; a printed square the child shades and physically folds, an array/doubling diagram drawn by hand, or a hundred square with multiples of 5 highlighted serve the same purpose for surfacing and explaining multiples patterns.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.9 requires identifying arithmetic patterns and explaining them using properties of operations (e.g. 4×n is always even, decomposable into two equal addends).
The multiplication square's diagonal symmetry embodies commutativity; explaining (not just noticing) patterns builds early mathematical reasoning.
Y4–Y5 pupils recognise and use number patterns; explaining patterns via structure supports mathematical reasoning.
learnerActions: Shade a chosen times-table on a multiplication square (e.g. shade every multiple of 5) and describe what you notice about the digits — for 5s, every product ends in 0 or 5.
Fold or reflect the grid across its main diagonal so a cell like 7×8 lands exactly on 8×7; observe that every cell matches its mirror.
State WHY the table is symmetric: because 7×8 and 8×7 are the same product (commutativity).
Pick a 4×n cell and split it into two equal addends (2n + 2n) to show why 4×n is always even.
Use a 'predict the next' prompt: extend a shaded pattern one or two steps, say what you expect, then check against the grid.
activities.intendedInsight: A noticed pattern can be explained from the structure of the operation itself — the table's symmetry is a consequence (and a picture) of commutativity, and 'always even' follows from decomposing into equal addends — so maths patterns are consequences of properties, not coincidences.

activities.title: Be the pattern detective: tell me WHY
feedback: If the child justifies 'even + even = even' with only a couple of examples, distinguish spotting from proving: show that an even number can be made entirely of pairs (groups of two), so putting two evens together still gives only pairs, with none left over.
If the child restates rather than explains, reply 'you told me WHAT — now tell me WHY it must be so' and prompt for the operation's structure.
Accept the answer when the reason uses structure, not when it repeats the observation.
activities.rationale: Because the objective is EXPLAIN, a Socratic dialogue that repeatedly asks 'why?' and refuses restatement targets the reasoning gap of restating rather than justifying. Spoken or written back-and-forth can serve this; dialogue alone lacks a manipulable representation, so it pairs well with a visual grid the child can point to.
sourceClaims: The multiplication square's diagonal symmetry embodies commutativity; explaining (not just noticing) patterns builds early mathematical reasoning.
3.OA.9 requires identifying arithmetic patterns and explaining them using properties of operations (e.g. 4×n is always even, decomposable into two equal addends).
learnerActions: State a pattern you have spotted (e.g. 'multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5', 'the sum of two even numbers is always even').

When a 'mathematician' partner accepts only a structural reason, give the WHY: for 5s, each step adds 5 and two fives make a ten, so the ones digit lands back on 0; for even+even, each even is made of groups of two, so combining them still gives groups of two.
Explain the table's diagonal symmetry using commutativity, and predict whether a pattern will still hold for a large case (e.g. 5×100) and justify without computing it all.
activities.intendedInsight: An explanation names a cause grounded in properties; a few examples suggest a pattern, but a structural reason shows it must always hold.

activities.title: Match the pattern to its reason (check your explanation)
feedback: If a restatement distractor is chosen, highlight that it repeats the observation without giving a cause, then point to the decomposition that supplies the reason.
For a wrong 'next in sequence', return to the repeating step (e.g. +5) and re-derive the next entry.
activities.rationale: A recognition/matching task can specifically contrast explanation versus restatement and confirm prediction, which is useful for checking. Selecting an explanation verifies that a child recognises structural reasoning but does not itself elicit the child's own constructed justification; use it alongside tasks where the child states the reason in their own words.
sourceClaims: 3.OA.9 requires identifying arithmetic patterns and explaining them using properties of operations (e.g. 4×n is always even, decomposable into two equal addends).
learnerActions: Given a pattern, choose the correct explanation from options that include a tempting restatement distractor — e.g. 'Why is 4×n always even?' with a restatement ('because it's in the 4 times table') versus the doubling explanation ('because 4×n is 2n + 2n, two equal groups').
Predict the next entry in a shaded pattern on the table and check it.

Decide whether a stated related pattern (e.g. 'odd + odd is always even') is true and identify the structural reason or counter-reason — odd + odd is indeed always even, because each odd is a group of twos plus one, and the two extra ones pair up.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to select or reject explanations — not just spot patterns — checks whether reasoning is structural rather than a restatement.

constraints: Always demand a structural/property-based reason, not a restatement — ask 'why does that happen?' and accept only a cause (symmetry → commutativity; 4×n even → doubling/distributive; 5s → half of 10).

Multiple-choice or matching tasks verify whether a child can recognise a correct explanation; they do not elicit the child's own independently constructed reasoning, so pair them with tasks that require stating the reason.

A static DIGITAL tap-to-reveal multiplication square anchors and showcases patterns well but does not let the child fold or decompose cells on the same surface; supply physical folding of a paper square, hand-drawing, or an interactive fold/split tool so the child builds the explanation rather than only reading it. (A printed paper square, unlike a fixed digital image, can itself be folded along the diagonal.)
Paper/card cutouts of the square have real thickness and can be folded physically; a screen 'fold' is an idealised model of the same reflection — both represent the diagonal symmetry.
Guard against over-generalising a pattern beyond where it holds without checking, and against treating a pattern as coincidence rather than a consequence of properties.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the CCSS-M 3.OA.9 claim and the NCETM claim as verified:false, and the DfE claim as verified:true; evidence strength is carried over unchanged and not independently confirmed here.

The original rated a third-dimension (3D) representation as adding no explanatory power for 2D-table patterns. This is a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; it has been omitted rather than asserted as universal. A 2D representation is proposed on the observable affordance that these patterns are naturally arranged in a table.

Self-audit of examples: 4×n = 2n + 2n (two equal addends) is correct; multiples of 5 cycling the ones digit 0/5 via the +5 step is correct (e.g. 5×70 = 350, 5×100 = 500); table symmetry from commutativity (a×b = b×a) is correct; even+even via groups of two and odd+odd = even are correct. No arithmetic errors found in the migrated examples.

probeDeeper: Why does adding 5 each time make the last digit go 5, 0, 5, 0?
Will 5 × 100 still end in 0 or 5? How can you be sure without working it all out?
Why is the sum of two even numbers always even — can you explain, not just check?
How could commutativity explain why the multiplication table is symmetric?
assess.correctAnswer: Every multiple of 5 ends in 0 or 5. A child reasoning well explains WHY: adding 5 each time flips the ones digit between 0 and 5 (5→10 ones-digit 0, +5→15 ones-digit 5…), or because 5 is half of 10 so two fives make a full ten. The explanation, grounded in the structure, is the target — not just noticing the pattern.

errorPatterns.pattern: notices the pattern but explains it only by restating ('because it's the 5 times table') — no structural reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: prompt attention to the +5 step: show the ones digit going 5,0,5,0 as you add five each time; that alternation is the reason.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: when asked why, child repeats the observation rather than giving a cause

errorPatterns.pattern: believes the pattern is a coincidence that might break for large multiples
errorPatterns.nextMove: reason from the repeating +5 step, which never changes, so the ones-digit cycle continues forever; test a large case to reassure.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child is unsure whether 5×70 or 5×123 still ends in 0/5

errorPatterns.pattern: over-generalises 'even + even = even' or other table patterns without checking the property behind them
errorPatterns.nextMove: distinguish spotting from proving: a few examples suggest a pattern; a reason using properties (an even is two groups, so two evens combine into groups of two) explains it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child asserts a related pattern (e.g. sum of two evens) as true but justifies by a couple of examples, not structure

responseLevels.gap: cannot spot the pattern, or 'explains' only by restating the observation.
responseLevels.full: identifies the pattern AND explains it using the structure (repeated +5 flips the ones digit; properties of operations), generalising to large cases and to related table patterns.
responseLevels.partial: notices the pattern reliably and believes it always holds but justifies only by examples, without a structural reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at the 5 times table: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30... What do you notice about the last digit of every answer? Now tell me WHY that pattern happens — why must every multiple of 5 end in 0 or 5?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Noticing the pattern is easy; the objective is EXPLAINING it using the structure of the operation. The reason tier separates a child who describes ('they end in 0 or 5') from one who explains ('because each step adds 5, and 5+5 makes a ten so it lands back on 0'). Empirical-only noticing is the partial level.
